title: Complexity of polymatroid query-size bounds
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Is computing the general polymatroid query-size bound NP-hard? Use the following exact comparison formulation and deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions. Given \(n\geq1\), a finite list \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) of rational logarithmic degree constraints and a rational threshold \(t\), let
\[P(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\Gamma_n,\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\text{ for all }i\},\]
where \(\Gamma_n\) is the cone of normalized monotone submodular set functions on \([n]\). Is the language
\[\mathrm{POLYBOUND}=\{\langle n,\mathcal D,t\rangle:P(\mathcal D)\geq t\}\]
NP-hard under the reduction convention below, when dimension and all constraints are part of the input?
why: A general polynomial-time procedure would make a broad information-theoretic relaxation available for query planning without enumerating exponentially many subset entropies. A hardness theorem would explain why the known algorithms require special dependency structure. Determining which conclusion is justified separates a useful compact optimization method from a bound whose direct formulation is mainly an existential certificate.
status_note: The 2022 source explicitly asks whether computing the general polymatroid bound is NP-hard. Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs, 3 April 2025, still describe general polynomial-time computability as open and distinguish their normal-function hardness theorem from the unrestricted cone. A bounded primary-source search checked on 16 September 2026 found no matching general resolution; the exact rational-threshold and Turing-reduction conventions are stated editorial choices, and absence of a located resolution is not a proof of openness.

progress.text: The seminar records Hung Ngo’s question about the general complexity and possible NP-hardness of the polymatroid bound.
The Optimizing Polymatroid Functions preprint reports polynomial-time optimization for simple constraints and NP-hardness for the distinct normal-function optimization.

Theorem 1.1 supplies a polynomial-size LP for simple constraints; Theorem 1.3 gives general-to-restricted reductions, and Theorem 1.4 proves hardness only for normal functions. The introduction and conclusion still leave general polynomial-time computability open.

sentences: Polymatroid query bounds maximize a normalized monotone submodular function subject to supplied degree constraints.
The obvious linear program has exponentially many coordinates even when its input constraint list is short.
The source explicitly asks whether computing this general bound is NP-hard, formalized here through exact rational threshold comparisons.
Simple constraints admit polynomial-time algorithms, while hardness for the smaller cone of normal functions leaves the general question unresolved.
An answer would clarify whether this broad database estimation framework can be computed efficiently from compact dependency descriptions.

definitions:
For \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a polymatroid function is a real-valued function \(h:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[h(\varnothing)=0,\qquad h(S)\leq h(T)\quad(S\subseteq T),\]
\[h(S)+h(T)\geq h(S\cup T)+h(S\cap T)\quad(S,T\subseteq[n]).\]
These conditions imply \(h(S)\geq0\). Their cone is \(\Gamma_n\). Coordinates may be arbitrary real numbers; functions need not be integer-valued matroid ranks or entropy vectors. A constraint \((X,Y,b)\) has \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\), and means \(h(Y)-h(X)\leq b\). An empty list, zero budgets, equal sets and repeated constraints are allowed. The zero function is feasible. Set \(P(\mathcal D)=+\infty\) for an unbounded objective; in that case every finite threshold is accepted. Otherwise the finite rational linear program attains a rational optimum, and equality with the threshold counts as yes.

The input explicitly lists the constraints, not the \(2^n\) values of a candidate function. Write \(n\) and the list length in unary, each subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and every rational as a binary integer numerator and a positive binary denominator with delimiters; the threshold numerator may be negative. Let \(L\) be the total number of bits. Invalid strings are rejected. This card fixes the usual rational logarithmic-budget bit model for the source's optimization question: numbers \(b_i\), rather than potentially enormous degree counts \(2^{b_i}\), are supplied. It does not assume unit-cost exact arithmetic on arbitrary real inputs. Comparison is exact, with no numerical tolerance, promise gap, fixed dimension or fixed constraint arity.

The database meaning is as follows. A full conjunctive query joins finite relations by matching common columns and returns all variable columns, with set semantics. A degree bound \(N\) limits how many distinct \(Y\)-tuples extend each fixed \(X\)-tuple. For a uniform random output tuple, conditional entropy is at most \(\log_2 N\), while the entropy of the complete tuple is the logarithm of the result size. Every entropy vector satisfies the displayed polymatroid inequalities, so maximizing over polymatroids yields a valid logarithmic upper estimate. The source's linear-program framework is formalized here with rational logarithmic budgets. No database instance is an input to POLYBOUND, and maximizing the actual finite join size is a different optimization problem.

A language lies in NP when yes instances have binary certificates of polynomially bounded length verified by a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. NP-hardness here means that every such language can be decided by a deterministic oracle Turing machine with access to exact POLYBOUND membership and worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\), for some constants depending only on the reduced language. An oracle query returns one membership bit; writing the query and all other bit operations count toward the time bound. Equivalently, it suffices to give such a reduction from satisfiability of Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause. Clauses are disjunctions of variables or their negations, and the formula is the conjunction of its clauses. This explicitly chosen Turing-reduction convention avoids changing hardness when the complementary threshold convention is used. No randomized reduction, advice or entropy oracle is allowed.

The full optimization has \(2^n\) subset variables and exponentially many monotonicity and submodularity inequalities, so explicit rational linear programming gives a terminating algorithm taking time at most exponential in a polynomial of \(L\). That upper bound does not establish NP-hardness. The issue is the cost in the compact input length; with \(n\) fixed the linear program has fixed dimension.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that POLYBOUND is NP-hard under the stated deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions, or a proof of the logical negation of that assertion. A positive proof must preserve the general polymatroid feasible cone and the finite input encoding, and establish correctness for every source instance. Hardness of a restriction on the admissible functions, such as the cone of normal functions, does not imply this claim unless a valid reduction to POLYBOUND is proved. A polynomial-time algorithm would settle the principal algorithmic side of the source's broader complexity question, but by itself proves the negation of NP-hardness only together with a proved separation of P from NP; an unproved separation must be stated as a conditional result. Neither an exponential-size LP formulation nor difficulty computing a different entropic bound is a negative algorithmic result for this problem.

source_formulation.text: Determine the complexity of computing the polymatroid bound; in particular, is the general computation NP-hard?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 7.2. The card retains its explicit NP-hardness question and fixes rational logarithmic inputs, exact comparison and polynomial-time Turing reductions.

context_blocks.text: The source asks both for the complexity of the polymatroid bound and, explicitly, whether it is NP-hard. The displayed yes/no target is this stated hardness question for the entire degree-constraint class. The companion entropic question concerns existence of any computation procedure; the polymatroid bound is already computable by finite linear programming.

Unlike minimizing one supplied submodular function, this problem optimizes over the values of an unknown submodular function. The constraint list is compact but a direct feasible function has exponentially many subset coordinates. Standard polynomial-time solvability of explicit linear programs therefore leaves the desired compact-input complexity unresolved.

A degree constraint is simple when its conditioning set has at most one variable. For this class, Im and coauthors give a linear program with O(k n²) variables and O(k n) constraints, and an efficiently obtainable derivation of the bound using Shannon inequalities. The 2022 preprint already reports the tractability breakthrough; the 2025 paper supplies the formulation and theorem locators used here.

Theorem 1.3 of the 2025 paper reduces the general problem to several apparently restricted degree languages, including constraints with conditioning sets of size at most two and total sets of size at most three. Its statement that these cases are as hard as the general case is a reduction result, not a proof that any of them is NP-hard.

The same paper does prove NP-hardness after restricting feasible polymatroids to normal functions. Such functions have the form h(S)=Σ_T w_T·1[S∩T≠∅], with nonnegative weights indexed by nonempty variable subsets T. This is a smaller cone; its constrained maximum can change when arbitrary polymatroids are permitted. The hardness therefore does not settle Question 7.2.
